planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root shrubs in early spring into well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; eastern prickly gooseberry is a woodland-understory native found growing wild in rocky deciduous forest across the eastern US and tolerates deeper shade than most fruiting shrubs.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; eastern prickly gooseberry is a native woodland shrub found scattered through rocky, deciduous forest understory from the Appalachians west to the Great Plains, distinguished from cultivated gooseberries by its densely bristly, spine-covered fruit and its genuine tolerance of significant shade, making it one of the few fruiting shrubs suited to a true woodland edible garden. Small, greenish, bell-shaped flowers in spring give way by midsummer to round, purplish-brown berries covered in soft prickly bristles that are removed by rubbing before eating; the tart-sweet pulp is used in preserves and pies much like other gooseberries once the spines are dealt with. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose thicket at a woodland edge, providing cover and fruit for wildlife as well as the gardener, and needs little care beyond removing the oldest canes every few years to keep new growth productive.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root shrubs in early spring into consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; swamp red currant is a cold-climate native of wet, mossy woods, streambanks, and boggy conifer forest across the northern US and Canada and needs steady moisture and cool root conditions to thrive.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; swamp red currant is a low, spineless native currant of wet, mossy northern woods, streambanks, and boggy conifer forest ranging from New England across Canada into Alaska, thriving in the cool, damp, shaded conditions typical of that habitat. Dangling clusters of small greenish flowers in spring ripen to bright red, tart currants in summer, smaller than cultivated red currants but usable the same way in jellies, syrups, and preserves, and readily eaten by songbirds if left unpicked. Because it comes from a cold, wet, northern habitat it struggles in hot, humid, or dry summer conditions and is best suited to gardens in its native cold-hardiness range with reliably moist, shaded, woodsy soil rather than a typical sunny fruit garden bed. Mulch with leaf litter to keep roots cool and moist, and expect a modest, informal, spreading shrub rather than a heavy commercial-style producer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in early spring into acidic, sandy to peaty, well-drained soil in full sun; northern blueberry is a dwarf, cold-hardy alpine and subarctic species native to exposed barrens, tundra, and mountain summits of northern New England and eastern Canada and needs excellent drainage plus reliably cold winters.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in early spring into acidic, sandy to peaty, well-drained soil in full sun; northern blueberry is a diminutive, mat-forming species native to windswept alpine barrens, coastal headlands, and subarctic tundra of northern New England, the Maritimes, and eastern Canada, where it hugs the ground to survive harsh, exposed conditions. Its small, sweet, powder-blue berries ripen in mid to late summer on a plant rarely taller than knee height, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a low, dense groundcover on lean, acidic soil. Because it is adapted to a short, cool growing season and needs sustained winter cold to perform well, it is a specialty planting for far-northern or high-elevation gardens rather than a general-purpose landscape blueberry, and it will not thrive in hot, humid summer climates. Grow it as a rock-garden or barrens-style planting in sharply drained, lean, acidic soil, and avoid rich garden loam or added fertilizer, which favor weeds over this slow-growing native.
